questions.stem: Read Passage A: "Above the traffic, on the flat roof of a twelve-storey block, Aster tended his hives. He had kept bees up there for forty years, long before the city decided rooftops were fashionable. Every morning he climbed the service stairs with his smoker slung over one shoulder, while below him buses sighed at the kerb and office workers hurried with their collars up. The hives stood in a neat row, painted the pale green of old garden gates. Aster moved among them slowly, deliberately, the way he had learnt as a boy in his grandfather's orchard. 'The bees know a hurried hand,' he said. 'They can smell impatience.' He lifted each frame with the care of a man handling letters from the dead. Not everyone approved. The management company had written twice, politely suggesting the hives were a liability. Aster kept the letters in a tin, unanswered, like wasps he had not yet decided to swat. Up here, among the humming boxes, the city's rules seemed very far away. When the first jar of honey went to the caretaker's wife, the complaints stopped. Aster said nothing about it. He just smiled at the skyline, wiped his hands on his overalls, and opened the next hive." Give TWO facts the passage states explicitly about Aster or his beekeeping.
markscheme: B1: any one explicit fact — e.g. he has kept bees on the roof for forty years / he climbs the service stairs every morning / the hives are painted pale green
B2: a second, distinct explicit fact from the passage (not a restatement of B1)
questions.modelAnswer: Any two explicit facts, for example: Aster has kept bees on the roof for forty years, and every morning he climbs the service stairs with his smoker. Also creditable: the hives are painted pale green; the hives are on a twelve-storey block; the management company has written to him twice.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). Which short quotation from the passage best shows that Aster handles the bees gently? Give the quotation and say why it fits.
markscheme: B1: a gentle-handling quotation — 'moved among them slowly, deliberately' or 'the care of a man handling letters from the dead'
B2: a reason tying the chosen words to gentleness — e.g. 'slowly, deliberately' shows unhurried care
questions.modelAnswer: 'Moved among them slowly, deliberately' — the two adverbs show an unhurried, careful manner, which is exactly gentle handling. Equally creditable: 'the care of a man handling letters from the dead', where the simile makes each frame precious and fragile.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). What can you infer about how Aster regards the management company's letters? Support your inference with one reference to the passage.
markscheme: B1: a valid inference — he is untroubled by the letters / quietly defiant / does not take them seriously
B2: a supporting reference — 'kept the letters in a tin, unanswered' or 'like wasps he had not yet decided to swat'
questions.modelAnswer: Aster is untroubled, even quietly defiant: the letters do not worry him enough to answer. The support is 'kept the letters in a tin, unanswered' — and the comparison 'like wasps he had not yet decided to swat' makes his dismissal almost playful.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). You are preparing a summary of how Aster responds to opposition. Select THREE points from the passage you would include.
markscheme: B1: he ignores the written complaints — the letters stay 'unanswered' in a tin
B2: he says nothing in his own defence ('Aster said nothing about it')
B3: he wins people over without arguing — the gift of honey stops the complaints
questions.modelAnswer: Three selectable points: he leaves the management company's letters unanswered in a tin; he says nothing in his own defence, even when the complaints stop; and he disarms his critics with a jar of honey rather than with argument.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). 'He lifted each frame with the care of a man handling letters from the dead.' Explain the effect of the writer's language in this line.
markscheme: B1: identifies the simile — lifting frames is compared to handling 'letters from the dead'
B2: connotations — such letters are precious, fragile and irreplaceable
B3: effect — the routine task becomes tender, almost sacred, revealing Aster's reverence for the bees
questions.modelAnswer: The line is a simile: Aster lifts each frame 'with the care of a man handling letters from the dead'. Letters from the dead are precious, fragile and impossible to replace, so the comparison charges a routine task with tenderness — beekeeping is made to look almost sacred, and Aster's reverence for his bees becomes visible.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). The turn in the passage is the four-word sentence 'Not everyone approved.' Explain TWO effects of this short sentence.
markscheme: B1: after a run of longer sentences its brevity lands like a blow — it signals the turn in the passage
B2: it introduces the conflict (the complaints) without detail, creating anticipation
B3: its flat, impersonal tone echoes the disapproval it reports
questions.modelAnswer: The sentence is short and blunt after much longer ones, so it lands like a blow and marks the turn from calm description to conflict. It also withholds detail — we are told only that disapproval exists — which creates anticipation, and its flat, impersonal tone mirrors the disapproval it reports. Any two effects, explained, earn the marks.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). What is the writer's attitude to Aster? State the attitude and support it with TWO different references to the passage.
markscheme: B1: the attitude — affectionate admiration / amused respect (accept close synonyms)
B2: a first supporting reference — e.g. 'the care of a man handling letters from the dead'
B3: a second, distinct reference — e.g. 'like wasps he had not yet decided to swat' or 'He just smiled at the skyline'
questions.modelAnswer: The writer regards Aster with affectionate, amused admiration. The tenderness shows in 'the care of a man handling letters from the dead', the amusement in 'like wasps he had not yet decided to swat', and 'He just smiled at the skyline' leaves him serenely victorious. Attitude plus any two distinct references.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 1). Rewrite this sentence in your own words, keeping its full meaning: 'Up here, among the humming boxes, the city's rules seemed very far away.'
markscheme: B1: the meaning survives — on the roof the city's rules or authority feel remote or irrelevant
B2: genuinely reworded — no more than two or three words lifted from the original
questions.modelAnswer: For example: 'On the roof, surrounded by his hives, the regulations of the city below felt as if they no longer applied to him.' The sense — the remoteness of authority — is kept, but the wording is new; a version that merely deletes words from the original would not earn the second mark.
